docs.title: Hands on Practical for Resting-state Functional Connectivity
docs.text:
For this hands on lab practice, we will be using data from sub-001 that you downloaded and processed for the previous block.

They should be located at ~/fmriLab/flankerData_n4/, and you should be able to navigate to it by doing cd ~/fmriLab/flankerData_n4.

You should also have the "skull-striped T1 image" saved under ~/fmriLab/flankerData_n4/sub-001/anat/

docs.title: What you will learn from this lab practice
docs.text:
• How to replicate this famous finding from Biswal 1995

  • Understand how to preprocess fMRI data for resting-state functional connectivity analysis

  • Understand how to extract and input a "seed" timeseries to search for brain regions that show resting-state connectivity with this "seed" region of interest.

docs.title: Step 1, preprocess resting-state fMRI data
docs.text:
We will use the steps you learned from last block to preprocess the resting-state data.

  • Let's use FEAT again to set up preprocessing

    • Go to the subject folder and launch FSL
      • cd ~/fmriLab/flankerData_n4/sub-001/func
      • fsl

    • In FSL GUI, open 'FEAT FMRI analysis'

      • Define scope of 'First-level analysis' to 'Preprocessing' at the top of the GUI
      • Select sub-001-task-rest_bold.nii.gz as input 4D.
      • Set output to ~/fmriLab/flankerData_n4/sub-001/func/rest_rmot.feat
      • We will delete the first 4 volumes in Delete volumes
      • Leave the High pass filter cutoff (s) to 100s

    • Go to the Pre-stats tab. We will do the following preprocessing

      • Motion correction with MCFLIRT
      • Select BET
      • Spatial smoothing of 6 mm
      • select Highpass

    • Go to the Registration tab, do the following:

      • Select Main Structural Image
      • Select the "brain extracted" T1 as the main structural image
      • Change to normal search and 12 DOF
      • For standard space, change to normal search and 12 DOF

  • Hit Go!

  • We then need to manually do "low-pass" filter. That is because FEAT does not support it (only does highpass). We have to do it via command line in the terminal.

  • Now open the terminal, move to the rest_rmot.feat folder you just made: cd ~/fmriLab/flankerData_n4/sub-001/func/rest_rmot.feat
  • Note, this might not work if you didn't save rest_rmot.feat under sub-001, in that case you have to find our where you saved it.
  • Then run this command: fslmaths filtered_func_data.nii.gz -bptf -1 2.5 filtered_func_data.nii.gz
  • Here we are doing lowpass filtering of 0.08 hz.
    • the -bptf option expects a high-pass sigma and a low-pass sigma, which can be caluclated by
    • highpass_sigma = 1 / (2.35 * TR * HP_freq) (we use "-1" because we already highpassed the data)
    • lowpass_sigma = 1 / (2.35 * TR * LP_freq)) (remember TR is 2s)
    • If interested in an explanation for this, see here: https://www.jiscmail.ac.uk/cgi-bin/webadmin?A2=fsl;fc5b33c5.1205

docs.title: Step 2. Locate a seed region of interest in fsleyes
docs.text:
• Stay in the preprocessed output folder ~/fmriLab/flankerData_n4/sub-001/func/rest_rmot.feat/

  • Locate the right motor cortex

  • Use fsleyes to open up the preprocessed structural image
    • file, add from file, goto reg, select highres
  • Also add the filtered_func_data
  • In the Overlay list panel, select filtered_func_data image
  • To navigate to the right motor cortex, enter the following x y z coordinate for scanner anatomical space: \ x=34 (top row), y=-12 (middle row), z=24 (lower row)
  • With the filtered_func_data selected, select View -> Timeseries, and you should see a timeseries plot on the bottom panel of fsleyes, like below

  • Now if you toggle UP the structural image, you can see the timeseries is from the hand "knob" area of the right motor cortex

docs.title: Step 3. Add another timeseries from the left motor cortex to see their coupling, or functional connectivity
docs.text:
• We will now add another timeseries in the same network, to see the coupling of the right and left motor cortex at rest
  • Scale the right motor cortex timeseries by selecting Plotting mode: Normalised
  • Add the normalised plot to be "fixed" in the timeseries window by clicking the + in the plot list and keep the line blue
  • Now select the filtered_func_data image again, and enter the following x y z coordinate for scanner anatomical space: \ x=-33 (top row), y=-33 (middle row), z=24 (lower row). Another timeseries will appear in normalised units.
  • Add the new timeseries to also be "fixed" in the timeseries window by clicking the + in the plot list and change the line color to red

docs.title: Technical Assignment: Demonstrate a completed exercise for our resting state right and left motor cortex plot, and add your own third region of interest
docs.text:
• Plot the right motor cortex as shown above in blue
  • Plot the left motor cortex as shown above in red
  • Pick a third region in the brain that you think should NOT have strong functional connectivity with the right motor cortex, and plot it in green.

docs.title: Lab: Group-Level fMRI Analysis in FSL FEAT
Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this practical, you should be able to:

  • Use the FEAT GUI to create a group-level map of task-related BOLD activation.
  • Locate and interpret group-level results using the FEAT HTML report and FSLeyes.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Access FastX: FastX remote login.

Prerequisite: You should have completed the first-level analyses for sub-001, sub-002, sub-003, and sub-004. Each subject should have a flanker.feat output directory.

In this lab, we will combine the four subjects' first-level results to examine the average activation for each of the six contrasts from the single-subject analyses:

  • Congruent > baseline (con > baseline)
  • Neutral > baseline (neu > baseline)
  • Incongruent > baseline (inc > baseline)
  • Errors > baseline (errors > baseline)
  • Incongruent > neutral (inc > neu)
  • Congruent > neutral (con > neu)

docs.title: 1. Open the group-analysis GUI
docs.text:
1. Open a terminal and move to your data directory:

    cd ~/fmriLab/

  2. Type fsl and select FEAT FMRI analysis.

  3. In the top-left menu of FEAT, select Higher-level analysis.

docs.title: 2. Data tab: Select input and output directories
docs.text:
• Keep Inputs are lower-level FEAT directories selected.
  • Set Number of inputs to 4, because we have four subjects.
  • Click Select FEAT directories and select the flanker.feat directory for each subject.
  • Keep Use lower-level copes selected. These correspond to the six contrasts specified in the first-level analyses.
  • Set the output directory within derivatives, naming the group-level output group_n4.

docs.title: 3. Stats tab: Set up the group model
docs.text:
• Select Fixed effects.
  • Select Model setup wizard.
  • Keep the default Single-group average model and click Process.

Why fixed effects? In this teaching example, we are estimating the average effect for these four participants. A fixed-effects analysis does not support generalizing the result to a larger population. We are using it to learn the group-analysis workflow with a very small sample.

docs.title: Inspect the group model
docs.text: Discuss: What does the red line represent in the group model? How does this model combine information across the four participants?

docs.title: 4. Post-stats tab
docs.text: • Leave the Post-stats settings at their defaults for this lab.

docs.title: 5. Run the analysis and inspect the report
docs.text:
1. Click Go to run the higher-level FEAT analysis.
  2. When the analysis finishes, open its HTML report. It may open automatically in your browser; otherwise, find it in your group-level output directory.

docs.title: Check the registration summary
docs.text:
• Open Registration summary.
  • Confirm that the expected four subjects are included.
  • Inspect the image overlays: are the brains aligned as expected in standard space?

docs.title: Examine the group-level activation maps
docs.text:
1. Open Results.
  2. Select Lower-level contrast 3 (inc).
  3. Compare your output with the example below.
  • Confirm that the expected contrast is displayed.
  • Look for plausible activation clusters and any obvious image artifacts.

docs.title: Examine the statistical results table
docs.text:
Click the activation image in the HTML report to view the corresponding results table.

Discuss: What information is reported in the table? How does it relate to the activation map?

docs.title: 6. Lab submission: Evidence of completion
docs.text:
Submit two PDFs from your higher-level FEAT analysis to the lab assignment on ICON.

  1. Registration summary PDF: Open Registration summary in your higher-level FEAT HTML report and print/save it as a PDF. The TA will check that the expected subjects are included and that the image underlays and overlays are aligned appropriately.
  2. Group results PDF for con > neu: In the higher-level FEAT HTML report, open the results summary for the con > neu contrast and print/save that page as a PDF. The TA will check that the analysis completed and that the expected contrast and statistical map are present.

Before submitting, verify:

  • Both PDFs come from the higher-level group analysis (group_n4), not an individual subject's flanker.feat report.
  • The registration PDF shows the expected input subjects and alignment.
  • The results PDF is for the con > neu contrast.
  • Both PDFs are readable and uploaded to ICON.

docs.title: Set up FSL in FastX
docs.text:
This page shows you how to setup your fastx linux environment to have access to the FSL program.

Access FastX through the remote login link below: https://fastx.divms.uiowa.edu:3443/

Accessing FSL The program we'll use for viewing and analyzing MRI data is called FSL. The program is installed for you already, but you each need to add "instructions" for the terminal to find it from your home account. These instructions are in a .bashrc file.

How to modify your .bashrc file to access FSL

  • Click on the terminal icon in your fastx desktop
  • If unsure what this looks like, hover over the icons in the top left of the screen with your cursor and click on the MATE terminal icon
  • At the prompt type gedit .bashrc
  • We've just opened the .bashrc file with the text editor program gedit

  • Add the following lines to your .bashrc file (copy/paste encouraged) 

    export FSLDIR=/opt/fsl
export PATH=${FSLDIR}/bin:\
${PATH}
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/opt/fsl/extralibs
. ${FSLDIR}/etc/fslconf/fsl.sh

  • Click Save

  • In the terminal type source .bashrc
  • Did it work?
  • In the terminal type fsl
  • You should see a gray menu box pop up

docs.title: First-level task analysis
docs.text:
By the end of this practical you should be able to:

  • identify the two nifti images that are INPUT to the task analsysis
  • set up preprocessing in the FEAT GUI
  • create and understand a model of task-related BOLD signal in the FEAT GUI
  • understand how to test for activation differences between conditions
  • understand how to check the quality of registration, motion, and activation maps

Open the FEAT GUI from the flanker data directory:

  • Open the terminal and type cd fmriLab/courseData_FA26/flankerData_n4
  • In terminal type fsl and click on FEAT FMRI analysis

Data tab in FEAT GUI:

  • On the Data tab, click Select 4D data and select your subject's fMRI flanker data
  • For example, subject sub-001's functional flanker data is in the func folder and named sub-001_task-flanker_bold.nii.gz
  • Set the Output directory as that subject's func folder. Do this by clicking on the yellow folder and selecting their func folder.
  • Name your output folder flanker.feat like the example below
  • Do not delete volumes or change the high-pass filter

Pre-stats tab in FEAT GUI:

  • Keep MCFLIRT on with the default reference volume
  • Keep slice-timing as None here
  • Keep BET brain extraction on for the functional data (yellow box means 'on')
  • Set spatial smoothing to 6 mm
  • Keep the highpass filter on
  • Do not turn on MELODIC ICA data exploration

Registration tab in FEAT GUI:

  • Select Main structural image to open that window
  • Set your skull-stripped _brain image that you skull-stripped as the main structural image
  • Change search options to Full search and 12 DOF

Setting up task model in the Stats Tab in the FEAT GUI:

  • Move to the Stats tab, first turn on Add additional confound EVs and then select the outliers.txt file in your beh folder as shown:

  • Next, click on Full model setup. Set up your model using tabs for each explanatory variable (EV) like shown below:

EV1:

EV2:

EV3:

EV4:

  • After setting up the EVs, stay in the Full model setup window and go to the Contrasts & F-tests tab. Set up the contrasts as below. Click Done when setup complete.

  • After completing the Full model setup you will get your task model!

  • The last tab in the FEAT GUI is Post-stats. We will leave the defaults on for now. The settings here are most relevant when we get to group-level analyses.

  • Click Go. When it's finished, the results will appear within your flanker.feat directory. Your html report will then include output of brain activation maps as previewed below.

docs.title: Lab: First-Level fMRI Analysis — Quality Control
Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing your first-level analysis in FSL FEAT, you will evaluate the quality of your results by examining:

  1. Registration: Are the functional and anatomical images aligned correctly?
  2. Pre-stats: Is head motion likely to compromise the analysis?
  3. Post-stats: Do the statistical activation maps appear plausible and interpretable?

The goal is to learn how to distinguish a successful analysis from one that technically completed but may have quality problems.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
Open the HTML report generated by your first-level FEAT analysis. Work through the checklist below.

For each section:

  • Check each item after inspecting the relevant figure.
  • Give the section an overall rating: Pass, Questionable, or Fail.
  • Briefly explain your assessment using observations from the report.

docs.title: 1. Registration
docs.text: Question: Are the functional, anatomical, and standard-space images aligned correctly?

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Functional to high-resolution (example_func2highres): Do the outer borders of the brain and major anatomical features align?
  • High-resolution to standard (highres2standard): Do the ventricles align reasonably well? Are the outer borders of the brain aligned?
  • Functional to standard (example_func2standard): Does the functional image appear to be in the correct anatomical location in standard space?

docs.title: What to look for
docs.text:
• The overall shape and borders of the brain should align.
  • The ventricles are useful landmarks for evaluating anatomical registration.
  • Small differences are expected, especially because functional images have lower spatial resolution.
  • Large shifts, rotations, or anatomical structures that do not line up are concerning.

Overall assessment: Pass / Questionable / Fail

Your observations: Describe any misalignment you observe. Is it minor or severe?

docs.title: 2. Pre-stats: Head Motion
docs.text: Question: Is head motion likely to compromise the analysis? Your functional voxel dimensions are 3.5 × 3.5 × 4 mm.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Inspect the motion plots: Focus on the bottom graph, which shows estimated head displacement in millimeters (mm).
  • Check the magnitude of motion: Approximately how large is the maximum displacement?
  • Compare motion with voxel dimensions: Is the displacement small or large relative to the dimensions of a voxel?
  • Look for sudden changes: Are there large spikes or abrupt changes in head position?
  • Consider overall motion: Does movement occur throughout the scan, or is it limited to a few time points?

docs.title: What to look for
docs.text:
• Motion is measured in millimeters, so you can compare it with the dimensions of your functional voxels.
  • Movement of 3.5 mm is approximately the width of one voxel in the x/y plane.
  • Even movement smaller than one voxel can affect fMRI results.
  • Sudden movements and repeated motion spikes are especially concerning.
  • Movement that occurs systematically during one task condition can create misleading activation patterns.

Important: There is no single motion threshold that guarantees good or bad data. Consider both the magnitude and pattern of movement.

Overall assessment: Pass / Questionable / Fail

Your observations:

  1. What is the approximate maximum displacement in mm?
  2. How does this compare with the voxel dimensions?
  3. Would you be concerned about this participant's motion? Why or why not?

docs.title: 3. Post-stats: Statistical Activation Maps
docs.text: Question: Do the statistical maps appear plausible and interpretable? The Post-stats section displays statistical activation maps for each condition and comparisons between conditions.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Inspect all statistical maps: Are maps present for each condition and comparison?
  • Look for blank brains: Are any statistical maps completely blank (no significant activation)?
  • Look for border activation: Do you see widespread activation along the outer edges of the brain, sometimes called a "ring of fire"?
  • Look for unusual spatial patterns: Do you see straight lines, stripes, or other patterns that do not resemble plausible brain activation?
  • Consider anatomical plausibility: Are significant clusters located within brain tissue and in regions that make sense for the task?

docs.title: What to look for
docs.text:
Plausible activation patterns:

  • Clusters located within brain tissue.
  • Spatial patterns that are reasonably consistent with the cognitive task.
  • Activation that is not dominated by the edges of the brain or obvious image artifacts.

Potential warning signs:

  • Widespread activation around the outer border of the brain ("ring of fire").
  • Straight lines, stripes, or unusual geometric patterns.
  • Large clusters that appear to extend outside brain tissue.
  • Activation patterns that appear dominated by motion or other artifacts.

Important: A blank statistical map does not necessarily mean the analysis failed. It may mean that no voxels survived the statistical threshold for that contrast.

Likewise, statistically significant activation does not guarantee that the signal reflects genuine neural activity.

Overall assessment: Pass / Questionable / Fail

Your observations:

  1. Which statistical map shows the most convincing activation pattern? Why?
  2. Are any maps blank or suspicious?
  3. Do you see evidence of motion contamination or other artifacts?

docs.title: 4. Final Quality-Control Assessment
docs.text:
After reviewing all three sections, consider the overall quality of the analysis.

FEAT section Pass Questionable Fail Registration ☐ ☐ ☐ Pre-stats: Motion ☐ ☐ ☐ Post-stats: Activation ☐ ☐ ☐

docs.title: Reflection Questions
docs.text:
1. Would you include this participant's first-level analysis in a group-level analysis? Explain your decision using evidence from registration, motion, and activation maps.

2. Which quality-control finding concerns you most, and why? Consider how it could affect interpretation of the statistical results.

3. Can an analysis complete successfully in FEAT but still produce invalid or misleading results? Give one example from the FEAT report.

docs.title: Key Takeaway
docs.text: A successful FEAT analysis is not necessarily a high-quality analysis. Quality control helps us determine whether the statistical results are trustworthy and whether they can be interpreted as meaningful brain activity.

docs.title: Lab Submission: Evidence of Completion
docs.text:
Submit two screenshots for sub-001 to the lab assignment on ICON:

  1. Task model: The FEAT design/model visualization showing the task regressors. Print and save as PDF your task model summary from your FEAT Report. The TA will check that the model was generated and that the condition timing looks reasonable.
  2. Completed FEAT report: The Post-stats section of the flanker.feat HTML report for the con condition. Print and save as PDF from your FEAT Report. The TA will check that the analysis completed and that the expected activation map was produced.

These PDFs demonstrate completion and allow a quick check, but they do not independently verify every FEAT setting. Use the checklist above to evaluate registration, motion, and activation quality.

docs.title: Before next class
docs.text: Once you've completed all the steps above for sub-001, repeat for sub-002 and sub-003 and sub-004. Example PDFs for their FEAT activation reports will be on our course ICON site. Before next class, you should have statistical maps for the same contrasts, in the SAME order, for all subjects.

docs.title: Skull stripping
docs.text:
By the end of this practical you should be able to complete preprocessing on your data with the following steps:

  • Use FSL's BET tool to remove the skull from a T1 image
  • Use FSLeyes to check the output of BET

Access FastX through the remote login:

https://fastx.divms.uiowa.edu:3443/

In the terminal, move to the folder where our downloaded data is:

  • At the terminal prompt, type cd fmriLab
  • Type ls and you should see the data you downloaded as a folder named courseData_FA26

Using FSL's Brain Extraction Tool (BET) to skull-strip:

  • At the prompt, type fsl
  • Click the BET brain extraction button on the FSL menu
  • We will use BET to do a brain extraction on the our demo participant
  • Set up BET with default options:
    • Click the yellow folder to select your T1 image with skull as your Input Image
    • FSL will automatically fill in the Output Image with the same filename as your T1 and _brain at the end
    • Expand Advanced Options
      • Select Output binary brain mask image
    • Select Go to run BET
    • In the terminal you will see text appear, that text shows how the GUI selections are translated into bash syntax for the fsl software to run the command
    • Finished will appear in the terminal when BET is done

Example of what your menu options should look like for these default settings:

Checking BET:

  • Use the GUI menu to open your T1 with skull and brain mask in FSLeyes
  • Move the mask image to be the top layer in your Overlay list
  • Change the color of the mask to yellow by selecting the Red-Yellow color scheme
  • Use the Opacity slider to make the mask semi-transparent so you can see the brain image in the background
  • Use this checklist:
    • Top of the brain: Does the mask cover the brain without missing sections OR spilling into the eyes or skull?
    • Bottom of the brain: Does the mask "hug" the brainstem without spilling into the throat?

Modifying BET settings:

  • Open or return to the BET GUI
  • An advanced option that often helps: use the dropdown menu to select Robust brain centre estimation
  • If your mask was too small or too large at the top of the brain, change the Fractional intensity threshold
  • If your mask was too small or too large at either the top or bottom of the brain, change the Threshold gradient

Example of what your menu options look like with modified settings for Robust BET and modified f and g setting, naming the file output to document f and g settings:

  • Work in small groups to change your -f and -g options to produce different outputs, explore a range of options to learn! You won't break anything, promise.
  • Take turns showing each other what happens when these parameters are modified and decide what you think would be a sweet spot of good settings for this image, and why.
  • Use your collective knowledge to setting on a good combination of -f and -g parameters to arrive at a good BET result.

Lab 2 assignment

Take two screenshots that demonstrate poor and good BET output

1. Take a screenshot of your poor BET on the T1, with a yellow, reduced opacity mask. Show a view in fsleyes that demonstrates poor brain extraction. 
2. Save your screenshot as `poor_bet.png`
3. Take a screenshot of your good BET on the T1, with a yellow, reduced opacity mask. Show the SAME view as shown for your poor result. Use the cursor settings and/or toggling on/off layers to help you show the same slices for both masks.
4. Save your screenshot as `good_bet.png`

docs.title: Viewing structural and functional images
docs.text:
By the end of this practical you should be able to:

  • Use the terminal to navigate to where your MRI data for this course will be
  • Open MR images with FSLeyes
  • Distinguish between structural and functional images in contrast, resolution, and dimensions
  • Use FSLeyes to identify the coordinates and intensity at the cursor location, and toggle images on/off
  • View the time series of a functional image and understand what it means

Access FastX through the remote login:

https://fastx.divms.uiowa.edu:3443/

First prep step: Make a folder for holding data for our labs.

  • Open your terminal by clicking on the icon showing a little black screen.
  • Type pwd. Where are you in the computer filesystem?
  • Type ls. What other files are here?
  • To make a new folder using the terminal, type mkdir fmriLab.
  • Move yourself into the folder with data by typing cd fmriLab.

Second prep step: Download some images.

Open terminal and move to your fmriLab folder:

  • Open your terminal application.
  • At the prompt, move to the bids directory in the terminal by typing cd ~/fmriLab/.
  • Copy/paste the following to download the data: wget -O courseData_FA26.tar.gz https://github.com/mwvoss/cognitive-neuroscience-fmri/releases/download/FA26-data/courseData_FA26.tar.gz
  • Unpack the download by copy/pasting this in your terminal: tar -zxvf courseData_FA26.tar.gz
  • Type ls and you should now see you have a new folder named: courseData_FA26
  • The contents of this folder include two sub-folders of sub-demo and flankerData_n4
  • We will discuss the BIDS file naming pattern and the two file types: .nii.gz and .json

Open FSLeyes:

  • Open FSLeyes by typing fsleyes &.
    • The & at the end tells the terminal to run this program in the background. Meanwhile, you still have access to the terminal to run other commands.

Open and view images with FSLeyes:

  • Click on File → Add from file.
  • Open the T1 image in the anat folder of sub-001 who is in the flanker data set: sub-001_T1w_defaced.nii.gz
  • Overlay the two additional images in that directory: sub-001_T1w_defaced_brain.nii.gz and sub-001_T1w_defaced_brain_mask.nii.gz
  • Use the up and down arrows in the Overlay list to put your _brain_mask.nii.gz image on top, followed by the _brain.nii.gz image
  • Select the _brain_mask.nii.gz image and change the color scale, then do the same for the _brain.nii.gz image
  • Use the eye button to toggle the images on and off to see what is different between them
  • With the mask image selected, reduce the Opacity with the slider option in top menu bar

Understanding the T1 image files: Try to answer these questions with your neighbors.

  1. "Defaced" means the face has been removed from the image. Why do you think we did that? How does the defaced image differ from the other image we added?
  2. Place your cursor at different places in the image. How does this affect the coordinates? Based on the coordinates you see, how many dimensions are there in the image?
  3. Go to the following voxel locations and record the intensity value for each coordinate (shown in the far right info box): (a) 94, 144, 139; (b) 57, 142, 139; (c) 69, 172, 139. How do the intensities vary with tissue type?
  4. View a histogram of all the intensities in the brain by selecting the _brain.nii.gz image and selecting View -> Histogram. How many "humps" do you see and describe in words how this relates to the T1 contrast.
  5. When and why might you use the skills introduced above for comparing layers of multiple images, such as changing color schemes, opacity, and toggling images on and off?
  6. What do you think the letters on the four sides of each view shown below mean?

Add a functional image on top of the structural:

  • Use the steps learned above to add a new image.
  • Add the file named sub-001_task-flanker_bold.nii.gz which is in sub-001's func folder.
  • Place the cursor somewhere in the brain and then toggle the functional image on/off using this button:

Try to answer these questions with your neighbors.

  1. Does the functional image have more or less anatomical detail than the structural T1 image?
  2. What kinds of tissues are the brightest and darkest?
  3. How many dimensions are there in the functional image?
  4. Use the menu at the top-left of your screen to view the BOLD time series for a voxel: View → Time Series. How does the time series compare inside vs. outside the brain? What do the numbers represent for the y-axis of the time series?

Example with time series viewer on:

Lab 1 assignment

Take a screenshot like the example above with the following showing:

docs.title: Lab: First-Level fMRI Analysis — Quality Control
Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing your first-level analysis in FSL FEAT, you will evaluate the quality of your results by examining:

  1. Registration: Are the functional and anatomical images aligned correctly?
  2. Pre-stats: Is head motion likely to compromise the analysis?
  3. Post-stats: Do the statistical activation maps appear plausible and interpretable?

The goal is to learn how to distinguish a successful analysis from one that technically completed but may have quality problems.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
Open the HTML report generated by your first-level FEAT analysis. Work through the checklist below.

For each section:

  • Check each item after inspecting the relevant figure.
  • Give the section an overall rating: Pass, Questionable, or Fail.
  • Briefly explain your assessment using observations from the report.

docs.title: 1. Registration
docs.text: Question: Are the functional, anatomical, and standard-space images aligned correctly?

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Functional to high-resolution (example_func2highres): Do the outer borders of the brain and major anatomical features align?
  • High-resolution to standard (highres2standard): Do the ventricles align reasonably well? Are the outer borders of the brain aligned?
  • Functional to standard (example_func2standard): Does the functional image appear to be in the correct anatomical location in standard space?

docs.title: What to look for
docs.text:
• The overall shape and borders of the brain should align.
  • The ventricles are useful landmarks for evaluating anatomical registration.
  • Small differences are expected, especially because functional images have lower spatial resolution.
  • Large shifts, rotations, or anatomical structures that do not line up are concerning.

Overall assessment: Pass / Questionable / Fail

Your observations: Describe any misalignment you observe. Is it minor or severe?

docs.title: 2. Pre-stats: Head Motion
docs.text:
Question: Is head motion likely to compromise the analysis?

Your functional voxel dimensions are 3.5 × 3.5 × 4 mm.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Inspect the motion plots: Focus on the bottom graph, which shows estimated head displacement in millimeters (mm).
  • Check the magnitude of motion: Approximately how large is the maximum displacement?
  • Compare motion with voxel dimensions: Is the displacement small or large relative to the dimensions of a voxel?
  • Look for sudden changes: Are there large spikes or abrupt changes in head position?
  • Consider overall motion: Does movement occur throughout the scan, or is it limited to a few time points?

docs.title: What to look for
docs.text:
• Motion is measured in millimeters, so you can compare it with the dimensions of your functional voxels.
  • Movement of 3.5 mm is approximately the width of one voxel in the x/y plane.
  • Even movement smaller than one voxel can affect fMRI results.
  • Sudden movements and repeated motion spikes are especially concerning.
  • Movement that occurs systematically during one task condition can create misleading activation patterns.

Important: There is no single motion threshold that guarantees good or bad data. Consider both the magnitude and pattern of movement.

Overall assessment: Pass / Questionable / Fail

Your observations:

  1. What is the approximate maximum displacement in mm?
  2. How does this compare with the voxel dimensions?
  3. Would you be concerned about this participant's motion? Why or why not?

docs.title: 3. Post-stats: Statistical Activation Maps
docs.text:
Question: Do the statistical maps appear plausible and interpretable?

The Post-stats section displays statistical activation maps for each condition and comparisons between conditions.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Inspect all statistical maps: Are maps present for each condition and comparison?
  • Look for blank brains: Are any statistical maps completely blank (no significant activation)?
  • Look for border activation: Do you see widespread activation along the outer edges of the brain, sometimes called a "ring of fire"?
  • Look for unusual spatial patterns: Do you see straight lines, stripes, or other patterns that do not resemble plausible brain activation?
  • Consider anatomical plausibility: Are significant clusters located within brain tissue and in regions that make sense for the task?

docs.title: What to look for
docs.text:
Plausible activation patterns:

  • Clusters located within brain tissue.
  • Spatial patterns that are reasonably consistent with the cognitive task.
  • Activation that is not dominated by the edges of the brain or obvious image artifacts.

Potential warning signs:

  • Widespread activation around the outer border of the brain ("ring of fire").
  • Straight lines, stripes, or unusual geometric patterns.
  • Large clusters that appear to extend outside brain tissue.
  • Activation patterns that appear dominated by motion or other artifacts.

Important: A blank statistical map does not necessarily mean the analysis failed. It may mean that no voxels survived the statistical threshold for that contrast.

Likewise, statistically significant activation does not guarantee that the signal reflects genuine neural activity.

Overall assessment: Pass / Questionable / Fail

Your observations:

  1. Which statistical map shows the most convincing activation pattern? Why?
  2. Are any maps blank or suspicious?
  3. Do you see evidence of motion contamination or other artifacts?

docs.title: 4. Final Quality-Control Assessment
docs.text:
After reviewing all three sections, consider the overall quality of the analysis.

FEAT section Pass Questionable Fail Registration [ ] [ ] [ ] Pre-stats: Motion [ ] [ ] [ ] Post-stats: Activation [ ] [ ] [ ]

docs.title: Reflection Questions
docs.text:
1. Would you include this participant's first-level analysis in a group-level analysis?

Explain your decision using evidence from registration, motion, and activation maps.

2. Which quality-control finding concerns you most, and why?

Consider how it could affect interpretation of the statistical results.

3. Can an analysis complete successfully in FEAT but still produce invalid or misleading results?

Give one example from the FEAT report.

docs.title: Key Takeaway
docs.text:
A successful FEAT analysis is not necessarily a high-quality analysis.

Quality control helps us determine whether the statistical results are trustworthy and whether they can be interpreted as meaningful brain activity.

Before next class, you should have statistical maps for the same contrasts, in the SAME order, for all subjects.

docs.title: Skull Strip the T1 anatomical image
docs.text:
By the end of this practical you should be able to complete preprocessing on your data with the following steps: * [ ] use FSL's bet tool to remove the brain from a T1 image * [ ] use FSLeyes to check the output of bet

Access FastX through the remote login: https://fastx.divms.uiowa.edu:3443/

In the terminal move to the folder where our downloaded data is: * A the terminal prompt type: cd fmriLab * Type ls and you should see the data you downloaded as a folder named flankerData_n4

Using FSL's brain extraction tool to skull-strip: * At the prompt type fsl * Click the "BET brain extraction" button on the FSL menu * Steps to set up BET * Click the yellow folder to select your defaced T1 image with skull as your Input Image * FSL will automatically fill in the Output Image to have the same file name as your T1 with _brain at the end * Expand Advanced Options * Select Output binary brain mask image * Select Go to run BET * Example default settings

Checking BET: * Use the GUI menu to open your defaced T1 and brain mask in FSLeyes * Use the Opacity slider to make the mask transparent so you can see the brain image in the background * Checklist * [ ] Top of the brain: does the mask cover the brain and not spill into the eyes or skull? * [ ] Bottom of the brain: does the mask "hug" the brainstem or spill into the throat?

Modifying BET settings: * Open or go back to the BET GUI * An advanced option that always helps: Use the dropdown menu to select Robust brain centre estimation * If your mask was too small or large at the top of the brain, change the Fractional intensity threshold * If your mask was too small or large at either the top or the bottom of the brain, change the Threshold gradient

docs.title: View structural and functional MR images with FSLeyes
docs.text:
By the end of this practical you should be able to: * [ ] use the terminal to navigate to where your MRI data for this course will be * [ ] open MR images with fsleyes * [ ] distinguish between structural and functional images in contrast, resolution, and dimensions * [ ] use fsleyes to identify the coordinates and intensity at the cursor location, and toggle images on/off * [ ] view the timeseries of a functional image and understand what it means

Access FastX through the remote login: https://fastx.divms.uiowa.edu:3443/

First prep step, make a folder for holding data for our labs: * Open your terminal by clicking on the icon showing a little black screen * Type pwd. Where are you in the computer filesystem? * Type ls. What other files are here? * To make a new folder using the terminal type mkdir fmriLab * Move yourself into the folder with data by typing cd fmriLab

Second prep step, download some images: * Copy/paste wget -O lab01_images.tar.gz https://osf.io/bprq5/download/ * Use commands introduced above to see what was downloaded * To unpack the download copy/paste tar -xvf lab01_images.tar.gz * Move yourself into the folder with data by typing cd osfshare

Open fsleyes: * Open fsleyes by typing fsleyes & * The & at the end tells the terminal to run this program in the background, meanwhile you still have access to the terminal to run other commands

Open an image with fsleyes: * Click on File -> Add from file * Open the file named sub-97-T1w_defaced.nii.gz * Overlay another file, open the file named sub-97-T1w_brain.nii.gz * Change the color scale of the top image to see what is different

Understanding the T1 image: Try to answer these questions with your neighbors

1.0. "defaced" means the face has been removed from the image, why do you think we did that? How does the defaced image differ from the other image we added? 1.1. What kinds of tissues are the brightest and darkest? 1.2. Place your cursor at different places in the image and see how it affects coordinates 1.3. In addition to the coordinate location of your cursor, what additional information is being shown here? 1.4. How many dimensions are there in the image? 1.5. What do the letters on the four sides of each view shown below mean?

Add a functional image on top of the structural: * Use steps learned from above to add a new image * Add the file named sub-97_task-flanker_bold.nii.gz * Place cursor in the brain somewhere and then toggle on/off the functional image using this button

Try to answer these questions with your neighbors

2.0. Does the functional image have more or less anatomical detail than the structural T1 image? 2.1. What kinds of tissues are the brightest and darkest? 2.2. How many dimensions are there in the functional image? 2.3. Use the menu at the top-left of your screen to view the BOLD timeseries for a voxel: View -> Time Series. How does the timeseries compare inside vs. outside the brain? What do the numbers represent for the y-axis of the timeseries?
